title: The Flirt Episode

jokes.text: That sign says 'applesauce.' No, I'm kidding. It says 'applause.'
jokes.setup: Hank is warming up the studio audience before taping, pointing to the applause sign
jokes.punchline: He pretends to misread it as 'applesauce' — a deliberately lame warm-up bit that satirizes the banality of pre-show audience prep
jokes.explanation: Works as character comedy: this is exactly the kind of limp warm-up joke a sycophantic sidekick would tell. The meta layer (it satirizes the whole apparatus of manufactured studio enthusiasm) elevates it above a straight bad joke. Rewatch bonus because you appreciate how it establishes Hank's role immediately.

dialogue.line: That sign says 'applesauce.' No, I'm kidding. It says 'applause.'

jokes.text: Remember, you're all a big part of the show — so the better you are, the better Larry is.
jokes.setup: Hank pitches the audience on their importance to the show
jokes.punchline: The framing inadvertently centers Larry, not them — the audience exists to serve Larry's performance, not the other way around
jokes.explanation: Dry observational comedy about the Hollywood ego machine — Hank is supposedly flattering the audience but the phrasing reveals exactly who really matters. Character-specific but not a huge laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Really. That's... You're very desperate.

jokes.text: Really. That's... You're very desperate.
jokes.setup: Larry is receiving extended, over-enthusiastic applause from the audience after his entrance
jokes.punchline: He breaks from the gracious host persona to dryly note the audience's desperation, puncturing the artifice of the talk-show applause ritual
jokes.explanation: Sharp and economical. The show's entire premise — the gap between performed warmth and actual contempt — crystallized in four words. 'You're very desperate' is the exact thought every talk-show host has but never says. High character integration: this is Larry, not any generic host.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Princess Di, it was announced in the paper today... has, evidently, rumored, I guess, bulimia. And this is true, I'm going to England. Hank, maybe you can help me on this, 'cause I'm not up on the protocol. I know you're not supposed to eat until they eat. Now, how would it work in this case?

jokes.text: Princess Di has bulimia. I'm going to England — Hank, maybe you can help me on this — I know you're not supposed to eat until they eat. Now, how would it work in this case?
jokes.setup: Larry announces Princess Diana's reported bulimia and frames a trip to England as a protocol dilemma
jokes.punchline: The etiquette question — you shouldn't eat before royalty — applied to a bulimic royal creates a darkly absurd logical knot
jokes.explanation: A solid topical joke with a clever structural twist — the social-protocol frame applied to a medical condition is genuinely inventive. Dark without being cruel. The Hank involvement is a nice touch (including him as a prop). Slightly bloated in delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: All I know is always use the small fork first.

jokes.text: All I know is always use the small fork first.
jokes.setup: Larry has asked Hank for etiquette advice about dining with a bulimic princess
jokes.punchline: Hank deflects the impossible question with completely useless, unrelated etiquette advice — the small fork
jokes.explanation: Beautiful economy. Hank's non-answer — confidently delivered, completely irrelevant — is the perfect expression of his character: he wants to seem knowledgeable and helpful but has nothing to offer. The small-fork specificity is key; a vague deflection wouldn't work nearly as well.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, boy.

jokes.text: 'Keep the day job' is the old joke. You look attractive tonight.
jokes.setup: Larry acknowledges his monologue jokes were weak (the Princess Di bit didn't land great)
jokes.punchline: He pivots from self-deprecation directly into complimenting Hank's appearance — the whiplash non-sequitur deflection is the joke
jokes.explanation: Works as a small character beat — Larry's vanity about his performance colliding with his need to press forward. The 'you look attractive tonight' redirect is a classic host-to-sidekick move used here self-awarely.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: 'Keep the day job' is the old joke.

jokes.text: Ross Perot has dropped out of the presidential race, proving again that if you have a silent T in your last name you cannot become president.
jokes.setup: Political news: Perot drops out of the '92 race
jokes.punchline: The 'silent T' rule — a fake political axiom that sounds like it could be real wisdom
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever construction — the 'rule' is invented but feels plausible enough to land. The follow-through with Tsongas and Truman is strong structural comedy, using the pattern to both confirm and subvert the rule. Good monologue writing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Ross Perot has dropped out of the presidential race... proving again that if you have a silent T in your last name... you cannot become president. Paul Tsongas... The silent T does not work. Harry Truman, yes... because his name isn't Harry Ruman.

jokes.text: We have a wonderful show. Don't judge it by the jokes.
jokes.setup: Larry wraps the monologue and pitches the guests
jokes.punchline: He preemptively acknowledges the monologue was weak — a direct fourth-wall-adjacent admission that punctures the talk-show promotional formula
jokes.explanation: Six words of pure comedic economy. The self-awareness here is what separates Larry Sanders from a real talk show — a real host would never say this. It's simultaneously a character joke (Larry's neurotic self-awareness) and a meta-commentary on the show itself. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We have a wonderful show. Don't judge it by the jokes.

jokes.text: Thank you. I would have voted for you, too, if you'd been in a movie.
jokes.setup: Larry tells Mimi he would have voted for her for an Academy Award; she returns the compliment
jokes.punchline: The reciprocal compliment is immediately undercut by the reminder that Larry is not an actor — the flattery loop collapses
jokes.explanation: Elegant reversal. The structure is almost perfect: match the compliment beat for beat, then drop the floor out. It's genuinely witty dialogue between two performers playing the talk-show flirtation game. Mimi's line shows she can hold her own, which is also character work.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I would have voted for you, too, if you'd been in a movie.

jokes.text: That's the prerequisite that's stopped me from winning an Academy Award.
jokes.setup: Mimi has just noted Larry hasn't been in a movie as a condition of her hypothetical vote
jokes.punchline: Larry plays it completely straight — as if the only thing between him and Oscar glory is this technical requirement
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan follow-through. Larry's narcissism is so well-calibrated here: he accepts the compliment fully and identifies the movie requirement as merely a technicality. Pure character comedy in an efficient line.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's the prerequisite that's stopped me from winning an Academy Award. There's some little, small print that says... you have to be in a movie to get a nomination.

jokes.text: Among other things, I would love to see how you do a nude scene.
jokes.setup: Larry and Mimi are discussing making a movie together; the conversation is ostensibly professional
jokes.punchline: Larry pivots from movie-making to asking about nude scenes — on live television, in front of millions — establishing the flirtation theme of the episode
jokes.explanation: The pivot is well-timed and establishes the episode's central comic engine. Larry's audacity on his own show — where there are no consequences — is classic character comedy. Sets up everything that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Among other things, I would love to see how you do a nude scene.

jokes.text: I can tell you, funny and yet sexy. Really? So we have nude, yet funny and sexy.
jokes.setup: Mimi claims she does nude scenes both funny AND sexy; Larry repeats the categories back
jokes.punchline: The formal enumeration — 'nude, yet funny and sexy' — makes the exchange sound like a business meeting, heightening the absurdity
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation of the flirtation. Larry's cataloguing tone ('we have nude, yet funny and sexy') is a good character beat — he's interviewing her like a talent scout while clearly interested on another level entirely.

dialogue.speaker: Mimi Rogers
dialogue.line: I do them... I can tell you, funny and yet sexy.

jokes.text: I'm an Aquarius. I think that would work. You're a fire sign. I'm an air sign. Air feeds the fire, fans the fire, strokes the fire.
jokes.setup: Larry asks Mimi's sign and pivots to astrology as a flirtation vehicle
jokes.punchline: The astrology metaphors keep escalating toward obvious innuendo — 'fans the fire, strokes the fire' — on live television
jokes.explanation: The slow-burn escalation through astrology-as-foreplay is good cringe territory. 'Strokes the fire' in particular commits hard to the innuendo. The bit rewards attention — you can watch Larry convince himself this is acceptable on-air content.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm an Aquarius. I think that would work. Is that right? Sure. You're a fire sign. I'm an air sign. Air feeds the fire, fans the fire, strokes the fire.

jokes.text: Easy. So... The more air that goes into... The harder one blows the air into the fire, the more... Flame, yeah. Heat, and... Explosions can result. And before you know it, there's no way to put it out.
jokes.setup: The astrology/fire metaphor continues to build toward increasingly obvious sexual innuendo
jokes.punchline: 'The harder one blows the air into the fire' and 'before you know it, there's no way to put it out' — both parties fully committing to innuendo they're pretending is about astrology
jokes.explanation: The fragmented dialogue ('Flame, yeah. Heat, and...') mimics the halting, mutually-constructed nature of flirtation — both people building the thing together. A little bloated but the shared escalation between Larry and Mimi is well-performed cringe.

dialogue.line: Easy.

jokes.text: And my rising sign is kindling, but, please... let's get back to the nude scene.
jokes.setup: The astrology metaphor has been running hot; Larry has a rising sign
jokes.punchline: 'Kindling' — a perfect invented sign that extends the fire metaphor to its logical endpoint — followed immediately by the blunt pivot back to 'the nude scene'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Kindling' as a rising sign is a genuinely inventive comic construction — it extends the metaphor while simultaneously exposing how absurd the whole astrology-flirtation scaffolding is. Then the pivot to 'let's get back to the nude scene' is perfect deflation: he abandons the conceit entirely and just asks directly. The economy is exceptional. This line could only come from this character in this moment.

dialogue.line: The harder one blows the air into the fire, the more... Flame, yeah. Heat, and... Explosions can result. And before you know it, there's no way to put it out.

jokes.text: Butt out.
jokes.setup: Hank has interjected 'I'm a Capricorn' into the flirtation, trying to insert himself
jokes.punchline: Larry dismisses him with 'butt out' — which works as both a dismissal and, given the preceding nude-scene discussion, a possible pun
jokes.explanation: Two words that do a lot of work. The dismissal of Hank is character comedy (his pathetic attempt to join the flirtation), and the possible double meaning in context of the nude-scene conversation gives it extra juice. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And my rising sign is kindling, but, please... let's get back to the nude scene.

jokes.text: Well, actually, three is kind of a crowd.
jokes.setup: Larry offers that Hank could be in the nude scene too
jokes.punchline: Mimi gently rejects Hank's inclusion by invoking 'three's a crowd' — her polished delivery confirms she's in on the game
jokes.explanation: Clean, economical, and shows Mimi playing the game skillfully. The implied acceptance of the two-person nude scene while rejecting the three-person one is a nice move. Not exceptionally original but well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm a Capricorn.

jokes.text: I can tell you that that has never stopped him before.
jokes.setup: Larry announces he is married, seemingly pumping the brakes on the flirtation
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately torpedoes Larry's virtue signaling by revealing his history — 'that has never stopped him before'
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy. Hank's line does three things: it exposes Larry's hypocrisy, it reveals their relationship (Hank has intimate knowledge of Larry's past), and it does it on live television in front of Mimi and the audience. The timing — immediate, no hesitation — makes it feel instinctive. Very good Larry Sanders line.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Butt out.

jokes.text: Now, let me make this clear — not only to Hank, but to everybody watching — I take my wedding vows seriously and love my wife and am totally committed to that relationship. Now, by nude, do you mean neither of us would be wearing clothes?
jokes.setup: Larry delivers an earnest, extended disclaimer about his fidelity — seemingly course-correcting after Hank's betrayal
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots back to the nude scene, asking for clarification on the parameters
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and a perfect encapsulation of Larry Sanders as a character. The buildup is beautifully extended — 'not only to Hank, but to everybody watching' suggests genuine sincerity and public accountability — then the pivot to 'by nude, do you mean neither of us would be wearing clothes?' is a devastating punchline. The question itself is superb: it sounds like it's seeking clarification but is transparently just re-engaging with the fantasy. The structure is near-perfect. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I can tell you that that has never stopped him before.

jokes.text: Because I've been tricked before and ended up being the only one. Usually it results in a call to the police and all hell breaks out.
jokes.setup: Mimi confirms that in the hypothetical nude scene, neither would be wearing clothes
jokes.punchline: Larry reveals a history of being the only one nude — implying prior incidents serious enough to involve police
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark escalation. The implied backstory (police involvement, 'all hell breaks out') suggests a pattern of behavior that is both funny and revealing of Larry's character. The casual delivery — matter-of-fact on live TV — is the key. Character-specific and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Now, by nude, do you mean neither of us would be wearing clothes?

jokes.text: We are out of time? Is that the signal? This is... I can't believe... I'm never gonna get to tell my Academy Award story.
jokes.setup: After an extended flirtation sequence, the segment is apparently ending
jokes.punchline: Larry laments being unable to tell his Academy Award story — the story was never the point; the flirtation was, making the 'story' a transparent pretext
jokes.explanation: A decent comic beat revealing Larry's investment in maintaining the encounter. The 'Academy Award story' was always a prop for the flirtation, never a real story, which is good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Because I've been tricked before and ended up being the only one. Usually it results in a call to the police and all hell breaks out.

jokes.text: That's the first time you've invited anyone back for two nights in a row. And that includes Hank.
jokes.setup: Larry invites Mimi back for a second night — ostensibly to finish her story
jokes.punchline: Hank points out this is unprecedented — and includes himself as a data point, highlighting his own subordinate status
jokes.explanation: 'And that includes Hank' is the line that makes this. Hank's self-insertion into his own humiliation is tragicomically perfect — he's pointing out his own disposability while apparently thinking he's making an interesting observation. Strong Hank character work.

dialogue.line: That's the first time you've invited anyone back for two nights in a row. And that includes Hank.

jokes.text: I'd like to apologize to Michael Richards of the Seinfeld show for running out of time. — What an asshole.
jokes.setup: Larry gives a gracious on-air apology to Michael Richards for getting bumped
jokes.punchline: Michael Richards, presumably off-camera or just off-stage, responds 'What an asshole' — completely puncturing the professional courtesy
jokes.explanation: Brilliant juxtaposition of performed warmth and genuine feeling. The public/private gap — Larry's polished apology vs. Richards' actual reaction — is the show's central DNA in miniature. The celebrity cameo adding the punchline is structurally elegant. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Michael Richards
dialogue.line: What an asshole.

jokes.text: Why is he inviting her back? I'm the one who got bumped.
jokes.setup: Michael Richards watches Larry invite Mimi back for a second night
jokes.punchline: Richards' pique — he's the one who was bumped, but Mimi gets the invitation — reveals the absurdity of the situation from the guest's POV
jokes.explanation: A good follow-up to the 'What an asshole' beat — extends Richards' grievance with logical consistency. The irony (she got his spot AND gets invited back) is clear and well-pointed.

dialogue.speaker: Michael Richards
dialogue.line: Why is he inviting her back? I'm the one who got bumped.

jokes.text: How do you come down from a show like that? — Jazzercise.
jokes.setup: Someone asks Larry how he unwinds after the excitement of the show
jokes.punchline: Jazzercise — delivered deadpan, the specificity of the uncool answer is the joke
jokes.explanation: Perfect one-word punchline. 'Jazzercise' is funny because of its specificity and the gap between the supposed glamour of the show and the prosaic reality of Larry's life. Economy is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mimi Rogers
dialogue.line: Jazzercise.

jokes.text: I am not so sure I should've invited her back. — It'll be fine. Special chemistry between you two.
jokes.setup: Larry expresses doubt about the decision to invite Mimi back
jokes.punchline: Artie's straight-faced observation — 'special chemistry' — is a darkly knowing understatement given what we just watched
jokes.explanation: Artie's role as the knowing enabler who will eventually become the voice of caution is well-established here. 'Special chemistry' is perfectly sardonic.

dialogue.line: No, but glad to hear the Russian lessons are working out for you.

jokes.text: I'm still gonna get paid, right?
jokes.setup: Larry apologizes to Richards for running long and bumping him
jokes.punchline: Richards' immediate concern is payment — cutting through any pretense of artistic collaboration or disappointment, it's purely transactional
jokes.explanation: A sharp industry joke — the underlying reality of celebrity appearances is money, not exposure or relationship. Richards cutting to 'still gonna get paid?' strips away the diplomatic niceties perfectly. Good economy.

dialogue.line: Try the veal. I don't care that they live in cages. It's out of this world.

jokes.text: We're gonna have a drinkski. Do you want to join us? — No, but glad to hear the Russian lessons are working out for you.
jokes.setup: Someone invites the group to 'the Smokehouse' for 'a drinkski'
jokes.punchline: Artie deadpans that he's glad the Russian lessons are working out — 'drinkski' as a pseudo-Russian suffix is the target
jokes.explanation: A small gem. Artie's wit is sharp and dry — the 'Russian lessons' callback to 'drinkski' is wordplay executed with perfect economy. Classic Artie: he doesn't miss a beat.

dialogue.line: You know, if Hank does well he gets a year's supply of Turtle Wax.

jokes.text: Try the veal. I don't care that they live in cages. It's out of this world.
jokes.setup: Artie is apparently recommending the restaurant
jokes.punchline: 'I don't care that they live in cages' — a breezy dismissal of animal cruelty in service of a good meal
jokes.explanation: Very Artie. The cheerful amorality — 'I don't care that they live in cages' as a food recommendation — is both funny and character-defining. Rip Torn's Artie operates by a code that has no room for sentiment, and this line captures it perfectly. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: So, do you fuck her on the desk or on the couch? I'm guessing the desk because Hank is on the couch... and I know you're not into that.

jokes.text: You know, if Hank does well he gets a year's supply of Turtle Wax.
jokes.setup: The conversation has moved backstage; Artie comments on Hank's situation
jokes.punchline: Comparing Hank's situation to a game-show consolation prize — Turtle Wax — reduces him to a contestant rather than a TV personality
jokes.explanation: A nicely cruel Artie line. Turtle Wax is the perfect specific choice — it's unglamorous, it's old-fashioned, it's a game-show cliché. Artie's casual contempt for Hank's career is well-expressed. The line also works as a meta-comment on sidekicks generally.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It'll be George Segal month.

jokes.text: Wife watches the on-air flirtation segment and asks: 'I should tell you, I'm married.' — It's not that that's ever stopped him before.
jokes.setup: Larry's wife is watching the broadcast at home; Larry delivers his married disclaimer on-screen
jokes.punchline: She gives the exact same response Hank did on-air — 'It's not that that's ever stopped him before' — which is both a callback and a devastating revelation that everyone knows
jokes.explanation: An exceptionally well-structured callback. The same line landing from the wife carries exponentially more weight than from Hank — it's not just a zinger, it's evidence that Larry's pattern is an open secret even within his marriage. The structural elegance (same words, different speaker, different stakes) is excellent writing. One of the episode's strongest moments.

dialogue.line: We've got nothing.

jokes.text: Let's see who Leno's... — No, no, honey. I want to see if she straddles you.
jokes.setup: Larry's wife is watching the on-air flirtation with Mimi; Larry tries to change channels
jokes.punchline: She refuses — she wants to watch to see if Mimi 'straddles' Larry, the discomfort entirely explicit
jokes.explanation: Sharp domestic cringe. The wife's refusal to look away and her blunt language ('straddles') indicates this is not the first rodeo — she watches with a mixture of jealousy and dark fascination. The power dynamic (she controls what they watch) is well-used.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: The heavy one has such a pretty face.

jokes.text: So, do you fuck her on the desk or on the couch? I'm guessing the desk because Hank is on the couch and I know you're not into that.
jokes.setup: Wife is directly asking Larry about his expected infidelity logistics
jokes.punchline: The clinical specificity — desk vs. couch — and the Hank consideration ('you're not into that') makes it both absurdist and devastatingly characterful
jokes.explanation: An extraordinary line. The wife's absolute certainty that infidelity will happen, combined with the logistical specificity (furniture selection, Hank's location) and the parenthetical about Larry's preferences, creates a portrait of a marriage that is both funny and deeply sad. 'I know you're not into that' is the killer detail — she knows everything. Very high character specificity and originality.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Actually, kindling is my rising sign. So we could build quite a fire there.

jokes.text: Two nights in a row? — Well, you know, I made a mistake. I'm sorry. I will bump her. She's as good as gone. — I don't want you to bump her. — No, I wanna bump her.
jokes.setup: Larry backtracks on inviting Mimi; his wife insists she doesn't want him to bump Mimi
jokes.punchline: The inversion — Larry now wanting to bump her, wife insisting he keep the invitation — creates a comic escalation where both people have switched positions
jokes.explanation: 'Bump' doing double duty here is nice, and the rapid position-reversal is good marital comedy — each person maneuvering for psychological advantage rather than actually solving the problem.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: This is like watching the Rodney King tape. Don't make me watch this anymore.

jokes.text: It's a bad precedent to set. The next thing you know, it'll be George Segal month.
jokes.setup: Larry argues against having Mimi back two nights in a row on professional grounds
jokes.punchline: The slippery slope ends at 'George Segal month' — the specificity of choosing a real, mildly second-tier actor as the worst-case outcome is absurdist and industry-savvy simultaneously
jokes.explanation: One of the sharper industry jokes in the episode. 'George Segal month' is funny because of the specificity — not a fictional person, not a hugely famous one either, but someone recognizable enough that the joke lands as insider booking commentary. The dread with which Larry says it is the key.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I have seen the hand on the hand done many times. I, myself, have done it with Gregory Peck. Trust me, I felt nothing.

jokes.text: Good night. Sleep well. I know I won't.
jokes.setup: The couple exchanges goodnights in their marital standoff
jokes.punchline: The aside — 'I know I won't' — delivered presumably as Larry has left or turned away, is a perfect dry coda to the scene
jokes.explanation: A well-timed closer for the home scene. The wife's awareness, resignation, and dark humor are all compressed into four words. Competent and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: All I'm saying is I've played this course before. I know right where it goes. Hand on hand, flirting backstage... and then I'm fuckin' 'em in Hank's Malibu pad.

jokes.text: Batman gets old. He's got the Bat-walker. He's got the utility truss. His mind is totally gone. He steps out of the Batmobile... And? And, and he... We've got nothing.
jokes.setup: A writer pitches an 'old Batman' sketch to Artie with growing enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: The sketch falls completely apart — 'we've got nothing' — after the promising premise of geriatric Batman accessories
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke about comedy writing itself — and a specific form of comedy-room failure where a premise outpaces the actual jokes. 'Bat-walker' and 'utility truss' are good absurdist details. The collapse to 'we've got nothing' after that build is structurally satisfying. Also a good satire of TV sketch development.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You don't want to do that. He's had septic problems with that place.

jokes.text: We've got nothing. [The Batman sketch dies in the room]
jokes.setup: The writers build up the Batman sketch with excitement
jokes.punchline: One of them admits 'we've got nothing' — the entire sketch was a premise with no payoff
jokes.explanation: A perfect meta-moment: a show about making television showing its writers failing. The build-up ('and then, and he...') followed by flat silence and 'we've got nothing' is a great structural anti-joke. The silence IS the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Tell them I have Dutch elm disease.

jokes.text: We had it all worked out. It was brilliant. — We had gold, Arthur.
jokes.setup: Artie shuts down the Batman sketch because Mimi is returning
jokes.punchline: The writers insist the non-existent sketch was 'brilliant' and 'gold' — despite having just admitted they had nothing
jokes.explanation: A nice callback that deepens the self-delusion of the writers. They've already admitted the sketch was empty, but in retrospect it was 'gold.' Good writers'-room satire.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Leno will be jealous. I think he's just got that has-been Julia Roberts on.

jokes.text: Larry, the Bangles want to reunite and they want to do it on your show. — I don't know. It's such a shame. The heavy one has such a pretty face. — Arthur, that's Wilson Phillips. — Or the Temptations. Can I talk to you? — Where the hell's Meat Loaf? Get him. Meat's a good boy.
jokes.setup: Artie discusses booking options while clearly not knowing or caring about the difference between musical acts
jokes.punchline: Artie confidently confuses the Bangles with Wilson Phillips, then pivots to the Temptations, then demands Meat Loaf — each escalating the oblivious chaos
jokes.explanation: 'The heavy one has such a pretty face' is both a specific joke and a character revelation — Artie's casual cruelty and his inability to keep bands straight is pitch-perfect. 'Meat's a good boy' is an excellent button. The escalating chaos of his booking logic is very funny and very Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I am not gonna ask her about when she lost her virginity... because then I'll have to tell mine, and it always embarrasses my sister.

jokes.text: Where the hell's Meat Loaf? Get him. Meat's a good boy.
jokes.setup: The booking discussion devolves after the Bangles/Wilson Phillips/Temptations confusion
jokes.punchline: Artie pivots to Meat Loaf with the affectionate 'Meat's a good boy' — treating a rock star like an obedient pet
jokes.explanation: 'Meat's a good boy' is a genuinely funny line. The reductive, patronizing language applied to a celebrity — 'good boy' — mixed with Artie's genuine affection creates Artie's signature tone. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Always embarrasses my sister, I say. Never mind. I get it.

jokes.text: I guess it was more important than I thought. Actually, kindling is my rising sign. So we could build quite a fire there.
jokes.setup: Mimi finds Larry to talk — apparently Beverly delivered Arthur's 'don't flirt' message
jokes.punchline: Instead of being embarrassed, Mimi leans into the callback — 'kindling is my rising sign' — turning the on-air bit into a private come-on
jokes.explanation: A well-earned callback. Mimi picking up Larry's own line and deploying it in private changes the register completely — what was a performance becomes a real invitation. The callback structure here has genuine dramatic weight, not just comedic recycling.

dialogue.speaker: Bert Crawley
dialogue.line: It seems these two colored fellas were sittin' on the porch... I don't think there's going to be enough time tonight. But this is a very funny joke! It'll make their hair giggle! I'm sure it's great. It doesn't have to be colored. We can make them Polack.

jokes.text: Right there. I'm flirting. — What flirting? — Look at the way I'm grinning there.
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are watching the taped broadcast back in the control room
jokes.punchline: Larry insists he can see himself flirting on tape; Artie can't see it — the absurdity of analyzing your own face for flirtation evidence
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy. Larry's ability to see his own guilt in his own facial expressions — and his determination to convict himself — is a neurotic and specific character beat. The meta quality (watching himself on tape) is very Larry Sanders.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oprah's actually a small, white Jewish man. But don't tell anybody.

jokes.text: This is like watching the Rodney King tape. Don't make me watch this anymore.
jokes.setup: Larry is forcing Artie to watch the tape again to identify flirtation evidence
jokes.punchline: Artie compares the repeated watching to the Rodney King tape — a topical, very dark joke about forced re-viewings of uncomfortable footage (the King verdict was very recent in 1992)
jokes.explanation: A genuinely audacious joke. Equating a talk-show host's flirtation tape with the Rodney King evidence tape is exactly the kind of dark, culturally-specific joke that defines Larry Sanders as premium cable comedy. The absurdity of the comparison + the timeliness (1992) + Artie's complete deadpan delivery makes this exceptional. It's also character-specific: Artie would make this comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're such a good actress that I thought you were serious for a second.

jokes.text: I have seen the hand on the hand done many times. I, myself, have done it with Gregory Peck. Trust me, I felt nothing.
jokes.setup: Larry insists 'hand on hand' is a definitive flirtation signal
jokes.punchline: Artie invokes Gregory Peck as his own counter-example — he's done it with Gregory Peck and felt nothing — the specificity and grandeur of Peck as the example is perfect
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The choice of Gregory Peck is extraordinary — not a random name, but a specific icon of gravitas and handsomeness whose inclusion implies Artie has operated at this level for decades. 'Trust me, I felt nothing' is delivered with the confidence of a man who has survived wars and Hollywood parties. This is pure Artie — it could ONLY be said by this character. High quotability, strong character integration. The casual heteronormative subversion (he did it with Gregory Peck and is using it to prove a point about female flirtation) adds another layer.

dialogue.line: Are you okay?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I have a rotator cuff problem. I threw it out during the monologue.

jokes.text: All I'm saying is I've played this course before. I know right where it goes. Hand on hand, flirting backstage, and then I'm fuckin' 'em in Hank's Malibu pad.
jokes.setup: Larry is explaining his theory of the inevitable outcome of the Mimi flirtation
jokes.punchline: The pattern culminates in the very specific detail of 'Hank's Malibu pad' — which implies Hank has functioned as a facilitator of Larry's affairs
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Hank's Malibu pad' as the venue is a great detail — it creates a whole backstory about the Larry-Hank relationship and Hank's complicit role in Larry's behavior. 'I've played this course before' is also excellent economy. This line deepens the world significantly.

dialogue.speaker: Bert Crawley
dialogue.line: You look so much thinner in person.

jokes.text: You don't want to do that. He's had septic problems with that place.
jokes.setup: Larry mentions he'll end up at Hank's Malibu pad
jokes.punchline: Artie's objection is not moral but practical — the place has septic problems — deflating any drama with a plumbing concern
jokes.explanation: A perfect Artie line. The joke operates on multiple levels: (1) he doesn't morally object to the infidelity, (2) his only concern is the plumbing, (3) 'septic problems' as a romantic deterrent is the most Artie possible construction. It could ONLY be this character. Maximum economy, pure character integration. Artie's pragmatic amorality is the show's secret weapon and this is one of its best expressions.

dialogue.speaker: Bert Crawley
dialogue.line: There's these two Jews sitting on the porch. One of them says to the other...

jokes.text: Tell them I have Dutch elm disease.
jokes.setup: Beverly asks if Larry will do a benefit for the Tree People
jokes.punchline: Larry declines by claiming to have Dutch elm disease — a tree fungal disease, not a human ailment — the specificity makes it absurdist
jokes.explanation: A great quick joke. 'Dutch elm disease' perfectly parodies celebrity benefit excuses — it's tree-themed (for the Tree People), it sounds vaguely real, and it's completely absurd as a human condition. The fact that he asks Beverly to relay this with apparent seriousness is the extra layer. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That's your philtrum. I know, 'cause it's very hard to cover up.

jokes.text: Leno will be jealous. I think he's just got that has-been Julia Roberts on.
jokes.setup: Artie is reviewing the guest lineup, satisfied with their bookings
jokes.punchline: Artie dismisses Julia Roberts — one of the biggest stars of that moment — as a 'has-been,' which is both absurd and a perfect expression of his inverted show-business hierarchy
jokes.explanation: The joke inverts the reality — Julia Roberts was enormous in 1992 — which either means Artie is completely wrong or that the show's pecking order (a soap carver from Minneapolis is newsworthy!) is deliberately absurdist. Either way it's very funny. The Leno rivalry adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Usually you take the keys by the third try.

jokes.text: I am not gonna ask her about when she lost her virginity because then I'll have to tell mine, and it always embarrasses my sister.
jokes.setup: Beverly hands Larry interview questions including one about Mimi's first sexual experience
jokes.punchline: Larry's objection is not that the question is inappropriate — it's that answering in kind would embarrass his sister, which implies a horrifying backstory
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. The structure is exceptional: the premise (Larry objects to a question) sets up what appears to be a professional concern, then the punchline ('it always embarrasses my sister') detonates something much darker. The joke doesn't explain itself — it trusts the audience to arrive at the implication — which is the mark of excellent comedy writing. It's character-specific (only Larry would say this), it's deeply dark without being explicit, and it's among the most quotable lines in the episode. The follow-up ('Never mind') is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That? I'm not gonna see that. You do that all day long anyway.

jokes.text: Always embarrasses my sister, I say. Never mind.
jokes.setup: Larry has just made a deeply uncomfortable implication about his sister
jokes.punchline: 'Never mind' — the total retreat, pretending nothing was said, which of course makes it worse
jokes.explanation: The button to the sister joke. 'Never mind' is the funniest possible follow-up — it acknowledges the implication by trying to un-say it, but the attempt is futile. The pause before it is presumably awkward and adds to the impact. Two words that perfectly extend a great joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mimi Rogers
dialogue.line: You are completely adorable when you can't take a compliment.

jokes.text: Tell her 'don't flirt,' please. — Don't say 'don't flirt.' You know what to tell her. Don't tell her it came from me, okay?
jokes.setup: Larry asks Beverly to tell Mimi not to flirt
jokes.punchline: He immediately contradicts himself — 'don't say don't flirt' — revealing he wants the message conveyed but can't acknowledge that he's sending it
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy. Larry's inability to commit to his own instructions — wanting to convey a message without being its author — is perfectly neurotic. The workplace comedy of sending a contradictory message through a subordinate is relatable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: 'Camptown Races.' I know that song. Sounds good to me.

jokes.text: Close it. Leave it open. Thank you.
jokes.setup: Larry gives Beverly contradictory door instructions as she exits
jokes.punchline: He asks her to close it, then leave it open, then thanks her for presumably doing neither or both — a small expression of his indecisiveness
jokes.explanation: A small but effective character beat. Larry's anxious indecisiveness extends even to door instructions — a minor but very true note about the neurotic temperament established throughout.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: She's singing 'Camptown Races' with a guy who carves soap. She's just being a good guest.

jokes.text: You know how many bars of soap it takes to make a Virgin Mary?
jokes.setup: Bert Crawley, the soap carver from Minneapolis, is being prepped for the show
jokes.punchline: The non-sequitur question about soap Virgins — posed as if it's fascinating — is funny because of how mundane the world of competitive soap carving is
jokes.explanation: Bert Crawley functions as a recurring absurdist element — the show's satire of 'civilian' talk show guests who exist in a completely different register from celebrities. The soap-Virgin question is good in context.

dialogue.line: Michelle Pfeiffer?

jokes.text: It doesn't have to be colored. We can make them Polack.
jokes.setup: Beverly tries to shut down Bert's racist joke; he offers to adapt it
jokes.punchline: His solution — switching the targets to Polish people — is offered as a generous accommodation, compounding the absurdity
jokes.explanation: The follow-up that makes the Bert sequence complete. His oblivious 'flexibility' — treating ethnic targets as interchangeable — is the perfect characterization of a certain kind of casual provincial racism. The economy is good and the joke is entirely about Bert's cluelessness.

jokes.text: Oh, it's you. — Hey, Hank. — You just get here? — Yeah, busy day. Up to my shorts. I was doing a commercial spot for Stanley Light Duty Hammers. — How'd it go? — What do you mean? It was fine. It was just a job. Got a check.
jokes.setup: Hank arrives on set; someone asks how his commercial went
jokes.punchline: 'What do you mean? It was fine. It was just a job. Got a check.' — Hank's defensiveness and resigned delivery reveals the gap between his self-image and his actual career
jokes.explanation: A portrait of Hank's diminished career in miniature. 'It was just a job. Got a check.' — from a man who presumably dreamed of more — is quietly devastating. The defensiveness ('What do you mean?') indicates he's been asked this before and doesn't enjoy answering.

jokes.text: Except nails. They said absolutely no nails.
jokes.setup: Hank offers that if anyone needs Stanley products, they should ask him
jokes.punchline: The catch — absolutely no nails — undermines the offer entirely and raises more questions than it answers
jokes.explanation: A superb small joke. 'Absolutely no nails' from a hardware company's spokesperson is logistically absurd and implies some kind of contract dispute or product line limitation that is never explained. The 'absolutely' intensifier makes it funnier. Perfect economy. The timing — delivered as an afterthought — is ideal.

jokes.text: I wear far less than any other talk-show host. Oprah's actually a small, white Jewish man. But don't tell anybody.
jokes.setup: Larry is heading to makeup and mentions he wears less makeup than other hosts
jokes.punchline: He pivots to claiming Oprah is secretly 'a small, white Jewish man' — a completely absurdist, inexplicable claim delivered in confidence
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it's entirely unmotivated — Larry just spontaneously drops this 'secret' about Oprah with no setup or explanation. The specificity ('small, white Jewish man') and the request for discretion add to the absurdity. Good Larry-specific comedy: his competitive relationship with other hosts expressed as conspiracy theory.

jokes.text: That's a great area, that artificial flirting thing. The audience loves that. — Did it seem artificial? — Well, you know, not artificial... but, you know, not real. — Oh, I was serious.
jokes.setup: Larry tries to explain away the on-air flirtation as a performance technique
jokes.punchline: Mimi flatly states she was serious — deflating Larry's escape hatch and dramatically raising the stakes
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured cringe beat. Larry's verbal squirming — 'not artificial... but, you know, not real' — is an attempt to occupy both positions simultaneously. 'Oh, I was serious' is devastatingly simple. The structure of the exchange is excellent: the audience sees Larry trying to escape, then sees the exit close.

jokes.text: Oh, man! I really thought... You're such a good actress that I thought you were serious for a second.
jokes.setup: Mimi has told Larry she was genuinely serious about finding him attractive; Larry clearly believes her
jokes.punchline: He covers with 'you're such a good actress' — trying to re-frame her sincerity as performance, even though he clearly now wants to believe her
jokes.explanation: Larry's transparent self-protection mechanism — denying what he wants — is very characteristic. The 'good actress' compliment as a defense is both funny and a little sad. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Are you okay? — I have a rotator cuff problem. I threw it out during the monologue.
jokes.setup: An emotionally charged moment is interrupted by Larry apparently wincing or moving strangely
jokes.punchline: He has a rotator cuff injury from the monologue — physical comedy from the most sedentary possible activity
jokes.explanation: A perfectly timed deflation of a romantic moment. 'I threw it out during the monologue' is absurd and very specific — injuring yourself during a seated TV monologue. The joke also humanizes Larry in the best possible way: just as things get real, his body betrays him. Excellent structural use of the interruption.

jokes.text: I wear far less than any other talk-show host.
jokes.setup: Larry is leaving Mimi's room; he mentions his makeup habits again
jokes.punchline: He's already said this exact thing earlier in the scene — returning to the line suggests he uses it habitually, like a calling card
jokes.explanation: The repetition is the joke — Larry has a stock self-promotional line about his minimal makeup usage and he deploys it reflexively, apparently unaware he's said it to the same person minutes earlier. A small running gag that reveals the performative habit.

jokes.text: I already told you that.
jokes.setup: Larry repeats the makeup line he already said
jokes.punchline: Mimi's flat acknowledgment — 'I already told you that' — [actually she means 'you already told me'] confirms he is using a stock line he's forgotten he used
jokes.explanation: Four words that expose Larry's performance completely. Mimi's gentle busting of his habit is both funny and humanizing for both characters. The economy is perfect.

jokes.text: I don't actually have his actual number. But I will give you this. — So this is... — This is my number. You can call me to get his number.
jokes.setup: Larry has offered Mimi a chiropractor's number; she moves toward the door
jokes.punchline: He admits he doesn't actually have the chiropractor's number — the whole offer was a pretext to give her his own number
jokes.explanation: 'You can call me to get his number' is a great construction — the chiropractor is now a fictional intermediary for a direct come-on. The two-step logic (call me to get the number to call him) is transparently absurd and very funny. Good structure.

jokes.text: You look so much thinner in person. — I'm Bert Crawley, soap carver from Minneapolis.
jokes.setup: Larry has just had a charged private moment with Mimi; as she leaves, someone compliments Larry on his appearance
jokes.punchline: Bert Crawley introduces himself in the same breath — the collision of the charged romantic moment with the mundane soap carver is pure tonal deflation
jokes.explanation: The cut from the romantic intensity back to 'I'm Bert Crawley, soap carver from Minneapolis' is a perfect tonal whiplash. Larry's private world crashes back into his professional reality in one line. The juxtaposition does all the work.

jokes.text: I also tell jokes. There's these two Jews sitting on the porch. — One of them says to the other... — Sorry, Larry.
jokes.setup: Bert attempts another of his jokes, this time targeting Jewish people
jokes.punchline: Beverly cuts him off again — this time the interruption is from Larry walking in, making the abort even more abrupt
jokes.explanation: The Bert joke-attempt is becoming a running gag — each time a new target group, each time cut off. The irony that the Jewish joke is cut off in front of Larry (who is Jewish) adds a layer. Beverly's 'Sorry, Larry' suggests she knows Larry's background.

jokes.text: She was standing right on top of me. I could count the little hairs on that groove under her nose. What do you call that? — This thing? What is that? — It's a cleft. — No, the cleft is your chin. — That's your philtrum. I know, 'cause it's very hard to cover up.
jokes.setup: Larry is describing Mimi's physical proximity backstage; they get derailed trying to name the area under the nose
jokes.punchline: Hank, unexpectedly, knows the word 'philtrum' — and knows it from personal experience with makeup coverage
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully digressive bit — Larry's romantic confession derailed by anatomy vocabulary. Hank knowing 'philtrum' from makeup issues is both character-specific and an unexpected moment of competence from him. The meandering quality mimics real male conversation.

jokes.text: I could count the hairs on the philtrum there. — you want the keys to my Place in Malibu? — No, I don't want the keys. — You sure? — No, I'm not sure, but I'm married.
jokes.setup: Larry is describing Mimi's closeness backstage; Hank offers the Malibu pad
jokes.punchline: 'No, I'm not sure, but I'm married' — Larry admits he's not certain he doesn't want the keys, which is an admission of genuine temptation
jokes.explanation: 'No, I'm not sure, but I'm married' is the episode's clearest statement of Larry's psychological state — the marriage is his reason, not his desire. The honesty of the admission is both funny and revealing. The Malibu pad callback deepens the series mythology.

jokes.text: I'm gonna catch up with him at home.
jokes.setup: Larry's wife learns he's in Mimi's dressing room
jokes.punchline: 'I'm gonna catch up with him at home' — the deliberate, controlled retreat, implying a reckoning will happen off-screen
jokes.explanation: Six words that carry enormous weight. The controlled understatement — 'catch up with him at home' — suggests both the dignified retreat and the implied domestic consequence. It's funny precisely because it doesn't say what it means. Economy is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: Hank, I'm not gonna fuck it up this time. — I'm really impressed. This is a new Larry. Usually you take the keys by the third try.
jokes.setup: Larry declares his fidelity; Hank has apparently offered the Malibu keys multiple times
jokes.punchline: 'Usually you take the keys by the third try' — Hank has a whole system for this, based on observed pattern
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. 'Usually you take the keys by the third try' implies Hank has a well-established protocol for facilitating Larry's infidelities — he's tried multiple times tonight and is tracking the attempts. The compliment ('this is a new Larry') makes it funnier: Hank is genuinely impressed by Larry's restraint, which says everything about the baseline.

jokes.text: If I feel you're getting into any dangerous flirting territory with Mimi, I'll make a signal like this. — I'm not gonna be able to see that. Like what? — That? I'm not gonna see that. You do that all day long anyway.
jokes.setup: Artie proposes a secret flirting-warning signal system for the taping
jokes.punchline: Whatever signal Artie demonstrates is apparently indistinguishable from his normal behavior — Larry points out 'you do that all day long anyway'
jokes.explanation: A great visual gag that reads even in transcript. The joke is that Artie's 'signal' is just something he already does, making it useless as a signal — which reveals both Larry's observational awareness and Artie's unselfconscious mannerisms. The physical comedy is inferred but the dialogue confirms it. High character specificity.

jokes.text: Did they like it? — They liked you. — As a matter of fact, my mother thought you were very cute.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Mimi's parents liked the show
jokes.punchline: Her mother found Larry cute — not the show, not both of them — just Larry, which is exactly what he wanted to hear
jokes.explanation: A small vanity beat — Larry's clear pleasure at being called cute by her mother is consistent characterization. Functional comedy.

jokes.text: Well, moms do like me.
jokes.setup: Mimi mentions her mother found Larry cute
jokes.punchline: 'Well, moms do like me' — Larry accepts the limited demographic with complete self-satisfaction
jokes.explanation: A perfectly economical character line. 'Moms do like me' is both self-deprecating (that's his demographic) and strangely proud. It's also a little sad — the appeal to maternal affection from a married man flirting on TV. High economy, strong character integration.

jokes.text: And, Bert... may I say, you're adorable when you can't take a compliment. Not that I'd given you one, but it's a feeling I have.
jokes.setup: Larry turns to Bert Crawley on the couch to include him in the compliment exchange
jokes.punchline: 'Not that I'd given you one, but it's a feeling I have' — Larry preemptively clarifies he hasn't actually complimented Bert while maintaining the fiction that he's being kind
jokes.explanation: A superb line. The structure is precise: Larry builds up to what sounds like a compliment, delivers something warm, then immediately undermines it by noting no actual compliment was given. 'But it's a feeling I have' is the perfect absurdist coda. This is host-comedy at its best — performing warmth while withholding it. High economy and very quotable.

jokes.text: Bert, didn't you have a joke you wanted to tell?
jokes.setup: Larry turns to Bert on live television
jokes.punchline: He's inviting Bert to tell the racist jokes that have been aborted multiple times backstage — either unknowingly or as a bit of airtime-filling desperation
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff — Larry unwittingly opening the door to the racist jokes Beverly has been suppressing all night. The audience knows what's about to happen; Larry doesn't. Good running gag structure.

jokes.text: How's your shoulder doing? Did you call my chiropractor?
jokes.setup: On-air second night; Mimi asks about Larry's shoulder
jokes.punchline: She's asking about 'her' chiropractor — the one Larry admitted he doesn't have, whose fake number he used as a pretext to give her his own number
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed callback — she's asking on live TV about the chiropractor he doesn't have, in front of his audience and his wife (who may be watching). The public airing of a private maneuver is good cringe construction.

jokes.text: My shoulder has been feeling much better. Thank you for asking, if I may say.
jokes.setup: Mimi asks about the chiropractor Larry doesn't have
jokes.punchline: 'Thank you for asking, if I may say' — the over-formal construction and the gratuitous addition of 'if I may say' is pure Larry Sanders verbal inflation
jokes.explanation: The 'if I may say' verbal tic is a nice Larry Sanders touch — over-formal language used to deflect and redirect. Small but character-consistent.

jokes.text: Let's watch Nightline. — How about a song? — A song! Bert, do you know any songs? — 'Camptown Races.' — I know that song. — Sounds good to me.
jokes.setup: Larry tries to divert the conversation; Mimi suggests a song; Larry turns to Bert
jokes.punchline: 'Camptown Races' — Bert Crawley, soap carver from Minneapolis, ends the flirtation episode by leading the panel in Camptown Races
jokes.explanation: The structural comedy here is excellent — the entire flirtation arc is interrupted and resolved by a soap carver from Minneapolis leading the group in Camptown Races. The absurdity of the song choice (extremely wholesome, extremely square) as the episode's resolution is perfect. Bert as the unlikely savior of Larry's marriage is a great comedic device.

jokes.text: You got out of it this time. — I did? — Yeah. She's singing 'Camptown Races' with a guy who carves soap.
jokes.setup: The Camptown Races sing-along has diffused the flirtation; Artie observes
jokes.punchline: 'She's singing Camptown Races with a guy who carves soap' — Artie's summary of the situation is a perfect dry denouement
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best closing joke. Artie's description — 'she's singing Camptown Races with a guy who carves soap' — is an extraordinary piece of comic compression. It summarizes the entire episode's absurdist resolution in eleven words. The deadpan delivery, the specificity of 'a guy who carves soap,' the implicit comparison to what might have been — all of it is perfect. Could only be said by Artie, in this moment, about this situation. Extremely quotable and the joke grows better on rewatch when you understand the full Bert-Crawley-as-Chekhov's-Gun structure.

jokes.text: She's just being a good guest. — Are you sticking up for her? — No, I'm not. — Are you? — No. I'm not sticking up for her. We're having an argument about Mimi Rogers. — Isn't that ridiculous? — Yes. — That's exactly my point.
jokes.setup: The Camptown Races has ended; Larry and his wife are apparently together backstage or at home, having an argument about Mimi
jokes.punchline: Larry lands on 'isn't that ridiculous? / Yes / That's exactly my point' — he uses the mutual acknowledgment of the argument's absurdity as his defense, which is itself absurd
jokes.explanation: Good marital comedy. Larry's logic — 'agreeing this argument is ridiculous is my point, therefore I win' — is both funny and very specific to a certain kind of conflict-avoidant male reasoning. The wife's 'yes' is delivered as agreement that actually changes nothing.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. I'm not gonna flirt anymore on television... anywhere else and television and anywhere.
jokes.setup: Larry makes amends to his wife after the Mimi episode
jokes.punchline: His promise — 'not gonna flirt anymore on television... anywhere else and television and anywhere' — is a hilariously tangled construction that reveals the difficulty he's having forming the commitment
jokes.explanation: The verbal stumble on the promise is perfect character work — Larry can't even form a clean commitment, the words coming out wrong. 'Anywhere else and television and anywhere' is the linguistic equivalent of a dog chasing its tail. Specific to Larry's psychology.

jokes.text: We'll take it one day at a time.
jokes.setup: Larry promises not to flirt; his wife responds
jokes.punchline: 'We'll take it one day at a time' — the AA/recovery language applied to marital fidelity implies this is a chronic condition requiring a twelve-step approach
jokes.explanation: The recovery-language framing is both funny and a little bleak. It positions Larry's fidelity as a day-by-day struggle rather than a given — which, given everything we've watched, is accurate. Good economy.

jokes.text: I'll see you tomorrow night. My guests will be Boyz II Men, Danny DeVito, and, oh, Michelle Pfeiffer. — Michelle Pfeiffer?
jokes.setup: Larry signs off the show with next night's guests
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'Michelle Pfeiffer?' — exactly echoing the episode's premise (attractive female guest, Larry's flirtation pattern) — suggests we're about to do this all again
jokes.explanation: An excellent episode button. Hank's two-word response to 'Michelle Pfeiffer' summarizes the entire episode's theme and implies the cycle will repeat immediately. 'Michelle Pfeiffer?' is a callback to the entire episode in miniature — we know exactly what Larry will do, Larry knows, and we're all complicit. The economy is near-perfect and the rewatch value is high (the pause before Hank speaks would land perfectly with a live audience).

tmdb_overview: Jeannie becomes very jealous and accuses Larry of flirting with a playful Mimi Rogers on the show.
